decks.title: Chemical Reactions and Equations — Part 1: Equations, combination and decomposition
goals: Spot the signs that a chemical reaction has taken place
Tell a chemical change from a physical change
Turn a word equation into a balanced chemical equation with state symbols
Classify a reaction as combination or decomposition
Give one example each of thermal, electrolytic and photolytic decomposition

slides.heading: Chemical Reactions and Equations
slides.body_md: Part 1 — what a reaction is, how to write and balance its equation, and two big families: **combination** and **decomposition**.

visual.alt: Balanced equation: magnesium burns in oxygen to form magnesium oxide
visual.caption: One line of chemistry tells the whole story of a burning sparkler wire.

slides.narration: Namaste! Have you ever watched a Diwali sparkler fizz with brilliant white light? That light comes from a metal, magnesium, joining with oxygen from the air. Something new is made, and that is a chemical reaction. In this lesson we will learn to spot reactions around us, write them as neat chemical equations, balance them, and sort them into types. Keep a notebook handy. Let us begin.

slides.heading: Physical change or chemical change?
slides.body_md: Ask one question: **is a new substance with new properties formed?**
columns:
**Physical change**

- No new substance
- Usually easy to reverse
- Ghee melting, sugar dissolving in chai, water freezing into ice

**Chemical change**

- New substance(s) formed
- Usually hard to reverse
- Milk setting into curd, an iron gate rusting, rotis browning on the tawa
slides.narration: When ghee melts in a warm kadhai it is still ghee. Cool it and it sets again. That is a physical change: the substance stays the same. But when milk sets into curd overnight, you cannot turn the curd back into milk. Tiny bacteria have made a new substance, lactic acid, which gives curd its sour taste. A new substance means a chemical change. So always ask: has something new been made?

slides.heading: Five clues that a reaction has happened
bullets: Change in colour
Gas given off (bubbles)
Change in temperature
A precipitate (insoluble solid) forms
Change in state

rows: A cut apple turns brown in the air
Idli batter rises and fills with bubbles as it ferments
A bucket of quicklime and water becomes very hot
Soap forms a sticky scum in hard water
Solid firewood burns away into gases and ash

visual.alt: Table pairing five signs of a chemical reaction with an everyday Indian example of each

slides.narration: Chemists are like detectives. They look for clues. A change in colour, like a cut apple turning brown. Bubbles of gas, like idli batter rising overnight. A change in temperature, like a bucket of quicklime getting hot. A solid called a precipitate appearing in a clear liquid. Or a change in state, like solid wood burning away into gases. One clue alone is not proof, but these signs tell you to look closely for a new substance.

slides.heading: Watching a reaction: burning magnesium
slides.body_md: Rub the ribbon with sandpaper first to remove the dull oxide layer, then hold it in tongs in a flame. It burns with a **dazzling white light** and leaves a **white powder**, magnesium oxide: $\ce{2Mg(s) + O2(g) -> 2MgO(s)}$.

slides.narration: Here is a reaction you can watch in the school lab. A strip of magnesium ribbon is rubbed with sandpaper to remove its dull coating. Held with tongs in a flame, it burns with a dazzling white light, the same light you see in sparklers. Do not stare at it. A white powder, magnesium oxide, collects on the watch glass. Light, heat and a new white solid: three clues of a chemical reaction in one experiment.

slides.heading: Quick check: spot the chemical change
slides.body_md: Which kitchen change makes a new substance?
slides.narration: Time for a quick check. Look at the four changes from a kitchen on your screen. Only one of them makes a new substance. Use our detective question: is something new formed, and can it easily be reversed? Choose your answer, then read the explanation, even if you got it right.

slides.heading: From words to formulae
slides.body_md:
A **word equation** names the substances: magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide.
A **skeletal equation** uses formulae: $\ce{Mg + O2 -> MgO}$.
Reactants go on the left, products on the right, and the arrow means "react to form".

visual.alt: Flow from word equation to skeletal equation to balanced equation to adding state symbols and conditions

slides.narration: Writing a whole sentence for every reaction is slow, so chemists use a short form. First, a word equation: magnesium plus oxygen gives magnesium oxide. Next, swap the names for formulae. Oxygen gas is written as O two, because oxygen atoms travel in pairs. This is called a skeletal equation. It shows who reacts and what forms, but it is not finished yet. Two more steps remain: balancing, and adding state symbols.

slides.heading: Why equations must balance
slides.body_md: **Law of conservation of mass:** atoms are neither created nor destroyed in a reaction; they are only rearranged. So each element must have the **same number of atoms** on both sides. In $\ce{Mg + O2 -> MgO}$ one oxygen atom has gone missing — the equation is not balanced yet.

visual.alt: Atom count for the skeletal equation Mg plus O2 gives MgO: magnesium 1 and 1, oxygen 2 and 1, so oxygen is not balanced

slides.narration: Think of atoms as Lego bricks. In a reaction you can pull the bricks apart and build something new, but you cannot make bricks vanish or appear. That is the law of conservation of mass. So an equation must show the same number of each kind of atom on both sides. Count our skeletal equation: magnesium, one and one. Oxygen, two on the left but only one on the right. Not balanced yet.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: aluminium meets oxygen
slides.body_md: Balance $\ce{Al + O2 -> Al2O3}$ (the thin protective layer on an aluminium kadhai).
bullets: Step 1 — count: Al 1 → 2, O 2 → 3. Oxygen needs a common multiple of 2 and 3, which is 6.
Step 2 — make oxygen 6 on both sides: $\ce{Al + 3O2 -> 2Al2O3}$.
Step 3 — now Al is 1 on the left and 4 on the right, so put 4 before Al: $\ce{4Al + 3O2 -> 2Al2O3}$.
Step 4 — recount: Al 4 = 4, O 6 = 6. Balanced. Never change a formula; change only the numbers in front.

visual.alt: Atom counts for aluminium and oxygen at each balancing stage, ending with four aluminium and six oxygen atoms on each side

slides.narration: Let us balance aluminium plus oxygen gives aluminium oxide. Oxygen is two on the left and three on the right. The smallest number both can reach is six, so write three before O two and two before aluminium oxide. Now aluminium is one on the left but four on the right, so put four before aluminium. Recount: four aluminium and six oxygen on each side. Balanced! Notice we only changed the big numbers in front, never the small ones inside a formula.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: the gas stove flame
slides.body_md: Cooking gas contains propane, $\ce{C3H8}$. Balance $\ce{C3H8 + O2 -> CO2 + H2O}$.
bullets: Step 1 — start with the biggest formula. C: 3 on the left, so write 3CO₂.
Step 2 — H: 8 on the left, so write 4H₂O (4 × 2 = 8).
Step 3 — O on the right: 3 × 2 + 4 × 1 = 10, so write 5O₂ on the left.
Step 4 — recount C 3 = 3, H 8 = 8, O 10 = 10. Balance the element that appears alone (O₂ here) last.

visual.alt: Balanced equation for propane burning in oxygen to give carbon dioxide and water vapour
visual.caption: Leave the free element (O₂) for last — it is the easiest to adjust.

slides.narration: Here is a smart order for balancing. Start with the biggest molecule, propane. It has three carbons, so make three carbon dioxide. It has eight hydrogens, so make four water molecules. Now count oxygen on the right: six in the carbon dioxide and four in the water, ten in total. Ten oxygen atoms means five O two on the left. Recount everything. Tip: leave a free element like oxygen for the very end, because adjusting it disturbs nothing else.

slides.heading: State symbols and reaction conditions
slides.body_md: Conditions such as heat, light, a catalyst, temperature or pressure are written **above or below the arrow**.
bullets: (s) solid
(l) liquid
(g) gas
(aq) dissolved in water — aqueous

visual.alt: Potassium chlorate decomposes on heating with manganese dioxide catalyst into potassium chloride and oxygen gas; catalyst written above the arrow and heat below
visual.caption: Manganese dioxide is a catalyst: it speeds the reaction but is not used up, so it sits on the arrow.

slides.narration: A balanced equation becomes even more useful when it tells us the physical state of each substance. Write s for solid, l for liquid, g for gas, and a q for aqueous, which means dissolved in water. If a reaction needs heat, sunlight, electricity or a helper substance called a catalyst, write it on the arrow. In this example, manganese dioxide speeds up the reaction but is not used up, so it sits above the arrow, with heat below.

slides.heading: Quick check: balance it
slides.body_md: Find the smallest whole numbers that balance the equation.
slides.narration: Your turn to balance. Iron reacts with chlorine gas to form iron chloride. Count each type of atom on both sides, decide which element to fix first, and choose the set of numbers that balances it. Remember, only the numbers in front can change.

slides.heading: Combination: many become one
slides.body_md:
In a **combination reaction**, two or more reactants join to form a **single product**: $\ce{A + B -> AB}$.
Before Diwali, painters add water to quicklime: it hisses and gets very hot, giving slaked lime for whitewash.
bullets: Burning coal: $\ce{C(s) + O2(g) -> CO2(g)}$
Hydrogen burning: $\ce{2H2(g) + O2(g) -> 2H2O(l)}$
White fumes: $\ce{NH3(g) + HCl(g) -> NH4Cl(s)}$

visual.alt: Quicklime, calcium oxide, combines with water to form slaked lime, calcium hydroxide, giving out heat

slides.narration: Our first family of reactions is combination. Two or more substances join to make just one product. Think of whitewashing walls before Diwali. The painter pours water on quicklime, calcium oxide. It hisses, bubbles and gets so hot you cannot touch the bucket. One product forms: slaked lime, calcium hydroxide, which is painted on the walls. Burning coal and burning hydrogen are also combination reactions. The tell-tale sign: only one product.

slides.heading: Decomposition: one breaks into many
slides.body_md: In a **decomposition reaction**, a single reactant breaks into two or more simpler products: $\ce{AB -> A + B}$. Breaking bonds needs energy, supplied as **heat**, **electricity** or **light**.

nodes.label: Decomposition: one reactant → two or more products

visual.alt: Decomposition branches into three kinds: thermal using heat, electrolytic using electricity and photolytic using light

slides.narration: Decomposition is the opposite pattern. One substance breaks apart into two or more simpler ones. Breaking things apart needs energy, and the energy can come in three forms. Heat gives thermal decomposition. Electricity gives electrolytic decomposition. Light gives photolytic decomposition. Over the next few slides, we will meet one example of each kind.

slides.heading: Thermal decomposition in a lime kiln
slides.body_md: Limestone (calcium carbonate) is heated strongly in a kiln to make quicklime for cement and whitewash. The heat must be supplied all the time.
bullets: One reactant → two products: decomposition
Needs constant heating: thermal decomposition

visual.alt: Calcium carbonate decomposes on heating into calcium oxide and carbon dioxide gas

slides.narration: Across India, lime kilns heat limestone, which is calcium carbonate, to very high temperatures. It breaks into two products: quicklime, calcium oxide, and carbon dioxide gas. One reactant, two products, and the energy comes from heat, so this is thermal decomposition. The quicklime goes on to make cement and whitewash. Notice how it links back to our combination slide: the same quicklime later combines with water.

slides.heading: Heating ferrous sulphate crystals
slides.body_md: Pale green crystals first lose their water of crystallisation, then break down. A **reddish-brown solid** (ferric oxide) is left, and gases with the **smell of burning sulphur** come out.

First, water droplets appear as the crystals lose water. Then the solid changes to reddish brown, which is ferric oxide, and gases leave with a sharp smell of burning sulphur. Those gases are sulphur dioxide and sulphur trioxide. Always point the tube away from people, and never sniff directly.

slides.body_md: Pass an electric current through water with a few drops of dilute sulphuric acid (to help it conduct). Bubbles rise at both electrodes. The gas at the **cathode (−)** is hydrogen; at the **anode (+)** it is oxygen. Hydrogen collects at **twice the volume** of oxygen.

slides.narration: Now let us use electricity. Two electrodes sit in water with a few drops of dilute sulphuric acid, which helps the water conduct. Switch on the battery and bubbles rise at both electrodes. The tube over the negative electrode fills twice as fast. That is hydrogen, because each water molecule has two hydrogen atoms for every oxygen atom. The other tube collects oxygen. Hydrogen burns with a pop; oxygen relights a glowing splinter.

slides.heading: Photolytic decomposition: light at work
slides.body_md: White silver chloride turns **grey** in sunlight as it breaks into silver and chlorine. Silver bromide behaves the same way, which is why old black-and-white photographic film worked, and why silver salts are stored in **dark bottles**.

slides.narration: Finally, light itself can break a substance apart. Spread some white silver chloride in a china dish and keep it in sunlight. Slowly it turns grey, because tiny grains of silver metal are forming and chlorine gas is released. Silver bromide does the same thing, and that is how old black-and-white camera films captured pictures. It is also why your school lab keeps silver salts in dark brown bottles.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: name the reaction type
slides.body_md: Count the reactants and products, then look for what supplies the energy.
bullets: Two or more reactants → one product: combination
One reactant → two or more products: decomposition
Then name the energy source: heat, electricity or light

visual.alt: Four equations classified by counting reactants and products: two combination reactions and two thermal decomposition reactions

slides.narration: Let us practise sorting. Look at the first equation: two reactants, ammonia and hydrogen chloride, make one product, so it is combination. The second: one reactant, zinc carbonate, splits into two on heating, so it is thermal decomposition. Do the last two yourself before reading the answer column. The trick is simple: count how many substances are on each side, then ask where the energy came from.

slides.heading: Quick check: what kind of decomposition?
slides.body_md: Think about where the energy comes from.
slides.narration: One more check. This question is about old camera film. Ask yourself two things: how many reactants and products are there, and what supplies the energy for the change? Then choose your answer.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1
bullets: A chemical change makes new substances; look for colour, gas, temperature, precipitate or state clues.
Word equation → skeletal equation → balanced equation → state symbols and conditions.
Balance by changing coefficients only, never subscripts.
Combination: many → one. Decomposition: one → many.
Decomposition needs energy: heat (thermal), electricity (electrolytic) or light (photolytic).

visual.alt: Summary table of combination and the three kinds of decomposition with their patterns and examples

slides.narration: Let us wrap up Part 1. A chemical change makes something new, and we spot it through clues like colour, gas, heat, a precipitate or a change of state. We write reactions as equations and balance them using only the numbers in front. Combination joins many substances into one. Decomposition breaks one substance into many, using heat, electricity or light. Look at the table once more and say each example aloud.

slides.heading: Exam tips: equations and reaction types
bullets: Never change subscripts to balance: H₂O cannot become H₂O₂.
Write oxygen, hydrogen, nitrogen and chlorine as O₂, H₂, N₂, Cl₂.
Add state symbols whenever the question asks for a "balanced equation with state symbols" — they usually carry marks.
For "name the type" questions, give the type AND the reason (e.g. "one reactant gives two products").
Electrolysis: hydrogen at the cathode (−), oxygen at the anode (+), volume ratio 2 : 1.
A typical 3-mark answer: observation (1) + balanced equation (1) + type with reason (1).
slides.narration: Here is how to collect every mark. Never change the small numbers inside a formula. Write gases like oxygen and hydrogen as pairs of atoms. When a question says balanced equation with state symbols, the symbols carry marks, so do not skip them. When you name a reaction type, add a one-line reason. And remember the electrolysis pattern: hydrogen at the negative cathode, twice the volume of oxygen. In a three-mark answer, examiners usually look for an observation, an equation and a type.

decks.title: Chemical Reactions and Equations — Part 2: Displacement, energy, redox and corrosion
goals: Predict whether a displacement reaction will happen using the reactivity series
Recognise double displacement and precipitation reactions and name the precipitate
Classify a reaction as exothermic or endothermic
Identify the substance oxidised, the substance reduced, the oxidising agent and the reducing agent
Explain corrosion and rancidity as oxidation and suggest ways to prevent them

slides.heading: Chemical Reactions and Equations
slides.body_md: Part 2 — metals that push each other out, partners that swap, reactions that give out or take in heat, and the oxygen story behind rust and stale chips.

slides.narration: Welcome back! In Part 1 we balanced equations and met combination and decomposition. Now we go further. We will see metals pushing each other out of solutions, chemicals swapping partners like a dance, reactions that warm up or cool down, and the story of oxygen that explains why iron gates rust and why chips packets are puffed up with nitrogen. Ready? Let us go.

slides.heading: The reactivity series: the stronger pushes out the weaker
slides.body_md: In a **displacement reaction**, a more reactive element pushes a less reactive one out of its compound: $\ce{A + BC -> AC + B}$. A metal can displace any metal **below** it in the reactivity series from its salt solution.

slides.narration: Imagine a game of musical chairs where a stronger player can always take the chair from a weaker one. Metals behave like that. This list, called the reactivity series, ranks metals from most reactive at the top to least reactive at the bottom. A metal higher up can push a lower metal out of its salt solution. Iron is above copper, so iron can push copper out. Copper cannot push iron out. You do not need to memorise every position, but know the common ones.

slides.narration: Here is displacement in action. A clean iron nail hangs in blue copper sulphate solution. After about twenty minutes, two things have changed. The nail is coated with a reddish-brown layer, which is copper metal. And the blue solution has faded to pale green, because it now contains iron sulphate. Iron, being more reactive, has taken copper's place. This is also why a farmer should never keep copper sulphate spray in an iron bucket.

slides.narration: Let us predict. Step one, find the free metal. Step two, find the metal inside the salt. Step three, compare them in the series. slides.narration: In displacement, one element pushes another out. In double displacement, two compounds swap partners, like two pairs changing partners in a garba circle. Both compounds are usually dissolved in water. If one of the new pairs cannot dissolve, it appears as a cloudy solid called a precipitate. Such reactions are called precipitation reactions. Keep an eye out for that solid; it is the clue.

slides.narration: Take a test tube of colourless lead nitrate solution. Add a few drops of colourless potassium iodide solution. Instantly, a bright yellow solid appears and slowly settles. That yellow solid is lead iodide, and it does not dissolve in water. The lead and potassium have swapped their partners. Potassium nitrate stays dissolved, so you cannot see it. Lead compounds are poisonous, so wash your hands after this experiment.

slides.heading: Precipitates to remember
slides.body_md: Not every double displacement gives a precipitate: in neutralisation, $\ce{NaOH(aq) + HCl(aq) -> NaCl(aq) + H2O(l)}$, the partners swap but everything stays dissolved.

visual.alt: Table of five precipitation reactions with the precipitate formed and its colour

slides.narration: Examiners love asking for the colour of a precipitate, so here is a short list. Barium sulphate is white. Lead iodide is yellow. Silver chloride is white and curdy. Copper hydroxide is blue. Ferric hydroxide is reddish brown. One caution: not every double displacement makes a precipitate. When an acid neutralises a base, partners swap, but the salt and water both stay as liquid. It is still double displacement.

slides.heading: Exothermic or endothermic?
columns:
**Exothermic** — gives out heat

- Surroundings get warmer
- Burning LPG, respiration, quicklime + water, rotting vegetable waste in a compost pit

**Endothermic** — takes in heat

- Needs energy supplied, or surroundings cool
- Lime kiln (CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂), photosynthesis, electrolysis of water
slides.narration: Every reaction involves energy. If a reaction gives out heat, it is exothermic. Exo means out. Burning cooking gas, the quicklime bucket, and even a warm compost pit are exothermic. If a reaction takes in energy, it is endothermic. Endo means in. A lime kiln needs non-stop heating, and plants need sunlight to make food. Most decomposition reactions are endothermic, because breaking a substance apart needs energy.

slides.heading: Energy inside living things
slides.body_md: Respiration releases energy from food, so it is **exothermic**. Photosynthesis stores the sun's energy in glucose, so it is **endothermic**.

visual.alt: Respiration: glucose reacts with oxygen in cells to give carbon dioxide, water and energy
visual.caption: Respiration — the reason your body stays warm.

slides.narration: Energy changes happen inside us too. When you eat rice or chapati, starch is broken into glucose. In your cells, glucose reacts with oxygen to give carbon dioxide, water and energy. This is respiration, and because it releases energy, it is exothermic. That energy keeps you warm and lets you run. Plants do the reverse. Photosynthesis takes in energy from sunlight to build glucose, so it is endothermic.

slides.heading: Quick check: hot or cold?
slides.body_md: Read the observation carefully: where is the heat going?
slides.narration: Your turn. In this question a test tube feels cold to touch while a reaction takes place inside. Think about where the heat is flowing, from the surroundings into the reaction, or out of the reaction. Then pick the best explanation.

slides.heading: Oxidation and reduction
slides.body_md: Oxidation and reduction always happen **together**, so such reactions are called **redox** reactions.
bullets: Oxidising agent: supplies oxygen or removes hydrogen — it gets reduced
Reducing agent: removes oxygen or supplies hydrogen — it gets oxidised

visual.alt: Table: oxidation is gain of oxygen or loss of hydrogen; reduction is loss of oxygen or gain of hydrogen

slides.narration: Now a pair of very important words. When a substance gains oxygen, or loses hydrogen, it is oxidised. When a substance loses oxygen, or gains hydrogen, it is reduced. These two always happen together: if one substance gives away oxygen, another must take it. So we call them redox reactions. The substance that gives oxygen is the oxidising agent, and the substance that takes oxygen away is the reducing agent.

slides.heading: Copper turns black, hydrogen brings it back
slides.body_md: Heating brown copper powder in air forms black copper oxide — copper is **oxidised**. Passing hydrogen over the hot black solid turns it brown again — copper oxide is **reduced**.

slides.narration: Let us see both halves in one experiment. Heat brown copper powder in a china dish. Its surface turns black because copper gains oxygen and becomes copper oxide. Copper has been oxidised. Now pass hydrogen gas over the hot black solid. The black colour slowly turns brown again, and water forms. Copper oxide has lost oxygen, so it has been reduced, while hydrogen gained oxygen and was oxidised. Oxidation and reduction, side by side.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: who is oxidised, who is the agent?
slides.body_md: Analyse $\ce{2CuO + C -> 2Cu + CO2}$ (getting copper from its oxide with charcoal).
bullets: Step 1 — track oxygen: CuO loses oxygen and becomes Cu.
Step 2 — so CuO is reduced; C gains oxygen to become CO₂, so C is oxidised.
Step 3 — the substance that gives oxygen (CuO) is the oxidising agent.
Step 4 — the substance that takes oxygen (C) is the reducing agent.

visual.alt: Table: copper oxide loses oxygen and is reduced, acting as the oxidising agent; carbon gains oxygen and is oxidised, acting as the reducing agent

slides.narration: Let us analyse one step by step. Copper oxide is heated with charcoal, which is carbon. Follow the oxygen. Copper oxide loses its oxygen and becomes copper, so it is reduced. Carbon gains that oxygen and becomes carbon dioxide, so it is oxidised. Now the agents, and here students often mix up. The oxidising agent is the one that gets reduced: copper oxide. The reducing agent is the one that gets oxidised: carbon.

slides.heading: Quick check: spot the reducing agent
slides.body_md: Follow the oxygen atoms.
slides.narration: Try this one about a blast furnace that makes iron. Follow where the oxygen goes. Remember, the reducing agent is the substance that takes oxygen away, and it is itself oxidised.

slides.heading: Corrosion: metals slowly eaten away
slides.body_md: **Corrosion** is a metal being slowly damaged by air, moisture or chemicals around it. Iron forms reddish-brown **rust**, hydrated iron(III) oxide $\ce{Fe2O3.xH2O}$, and needs **both oxygen and water**. Copper gets a green coating; silver turns black (silver sulphide).

slides.narration: Have you seen the reddish-brown flakes on an old iron gate? That is rust. Look at this experiment. In tube A, the nail has both air and water, and it rusts. In tube B, the water was boiled to remove air, and oil stops fresh air entering, so no rust. In tube C, calcium chloride keeps the air dry, so again no rust. Iron needs both oxygen and water to rust. Copper turns green and silver turns black for similar reasons.

slides.heading: Stopping rust
slides.body_md: Every method keeps **oxygen and moisture** away from the iron surface, or uses a metal that resists them.

rows: Oil film blocks air and water
Zinc coating protects iron, even if scratched

visual.alt: Table of five rust-prevention methods, how each protects iron and an everyday example

slides.narration: Corrosion costs a lot of money every year, so we fight it. The idea is simple: keep oxygen and water away. Paint your gate. Oil your cycle chain. Coat iron with zinc, called galvanising, as in GI pipes and buckets. Even if a galvanised surface gets scratched, the zinc still protects the iron. Plate taps with chromium. Or mix iron with other metals to make stainless steel, like your steel tiffin box.

slides.heading: Rancidity: when oil goes off
slides.body_md: When fats and oils in food are **oxidised**, the food smells and tastes stale. This is **rancidity**.
bullets: Airtight containers
Packets flushed with nitrogen (chips, namkeen)
Antioxidants added to food
Refrigeration, and storing away from sunlight

nodes.label: Oxygen from air (helped by light and warmth)

visual.alt: Flow: fats and oils in food exposed to oxygen, helped by light and warmth, are oxidised and become rancid with bad smell and taste

slides.narration: Leave a bowl of namkeen open for a week and it starts to smell and taste odd. Oxygen in the air has reacted with the oils in it. This is rancidity, and it is also oxidation. To slow it down, store food in airtight containers, keep it cool and away from sunlight, and add antioxidants. That puffy chips packet is filled with nitrogen, an unreactive gas, so there is very little oxygen inside to attack the oil.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: one reaction, many labels
slides.body_md: Classify $\ce{Fe2O3 + 2Al -> Al2O3 + 2Fe}$, used to weld railway tracks. Ask each question in turn.
bullets: Displacement: aluminium (more reactive) replaces iron
Redox: Fe₂O₃ loses oxygen (reduced); Al gains oxygen (oxidised)
Exothermic: so much heat that the iron forms molten

nodes.label: Two or more reactants → one product?
One reactant → two or more products?
An element replaces another in a compound?
Also: oxygen or hydrogen transferred? Heat given out or taken in?

visual.alt: Decision flow for classifying a reaction: combination, decomposition, displacement or double displacement, then checking for redox and energy change

slides.narration: One reaction can wear several labels. Railway workers weld tracks using iron oxide and aluminium powder. Walk down the questions. Is there just one product? No. Just one reactant? No. Does an element replace another? Yes, aluminium replaces iron, so it is displacement. Now ask the extra questions. Oxygen moves from iron oxide to aluminium, so it is also redox. And it releases so much heat that the iron comes out molten, so it is exothermic too.

slides.heading: Quick check: the nitrogen in your chips packet
slides.body_md: Think about what oxygen does to oil.
slides.narration: Last check. A snack company fills its packets with nitrogen. What would happen if they used ordinary air instead? Think about what oxygen does to the oil in fried snacks, then choose.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 2
bullets: Displacement: a more reactive metal pushes a less reactive one out of its salt solution.
Double displacement: two compounds swap partners; an insoluble product is a precipitate.
Exothermic gives out heat; endothermic takes it in.
Oxidation = gain of O or loss of H; reduction = loss of O or gain of H; they happen together.
Corrosion and rancidity are unwanted oxidation; keep out air and moisture.

visual.alt: Summary table of displacement, double displacement, energy change and redox with key signs and examples

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 2. A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one. In double displacement, partners swap, and an insoluble product appears as a precipitate. Exothermic reactions give out heat; endothermic ones take it in. Oxidation means gaining oxygen or losing hydrogen, reduction is the reverse, and they always go together. Rusting and rancidity are both oxidation that we try to prevent by keeping out air and moisture.

slides.heading: Exam tips: types, redox and corrosion
bullets: Displacement vs double displacement: is a free element a reactant? Then it is displacement.
For redox questions, name all four: substance oxidised, substance reduced, oxidising agent, reducing agent.
The oxidising agent is itself reduced — the most common mix-up.
Always state the colour of a precipitate and of solutions (blue → pale green; blue → colourless).
Rusting needs both air (oxygen) and water; say both for the mark.
In 5-mark answers, use labelled diagrams and equations: they earn marks quickly.
slides.narration: Final tips for Part 2. If a free element is a reactant, think displacement; if two compounds swap, double displacement. In redox questions, name all four: oxidised, reduced, oxidising agent and reducing agent. Remember, the oxidising agent is the one that gets reduced. Mention colours wherever you can, because many marking schemes give a mark for the observation. For rusting, write both air and water. And in long answers, a neat labelled diagram is a fast way to earn marks.

notes.title: Chemical Reactions and Equations — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Chemical reactions and how to recognise them
sections.body_md:
A **chemical reaction** turns one or more substances (**reactants**) into new substances (**products**) with different properties. A **physical change** alters only the form or state; no new substance forms and it is usually easy to reverse (melting ghee, dissolving sugar, freezing water).

**Signs that a reaction has happened** — look for one or more of:
- a **change in colour** (a cut apple browning; blue copper sulphate fading when iron is added)
- **evolution of a gas** (bubbles in fermenting idli batter; fizzing of an antacid tablet in water)
- a **change in temperature** (quicklime and water getting hot)
- formation of a **precipitate** (soap scum in hard water; yellow lead iodide)
- a **change in state** (wood burning away into gases and ash)

One sign alone is not proof — ice melting changes state but is physical. Always ask: *is a new substance formed?*

**Burning magnesium**: a ribbon rubbed clean with sandpaper (to remove the oxide coating) burns with a dazzling white flame and leaves white magnesium oxide powder. Light, heat and a new white solid all point to a chemical change.

key_terms.definition_md: A substance that takes part in a reaction; written on the left of the arrow.
A new substance formed in a reaction; written on the right of the arrow.
An insoluble solid that separates out from a solution during a reaction.
A change in form or state in which no new substance is formed.

sections.heading: 2. Writing and balancing chemical equations
sections.body_md:
**Word equation** → **skeletal equation** (formulae, not yet balanced) → **balanced equation** → add **state symbols** and **conditions**.

**Why balance?** The **law of conservation of mass**: mass is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction, so the number of atoms of each element must be the same on both sides.

**Hit-and-trial method**
1. Write correct formulae; list the atoms of each element on both sides.
2. Start with the compound that has the most atoms; balance one element at a time using **coefficients** (numbers in front).
3. Leave free elements such as $\ce{O2}$ or $\ce{H2}$ for last.
4. Recount every element. Use the smallest whole numbers.
5. **Never change subscripts** — that would change the substance.

**State symbols**: (s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas, (aq) aqueous solution. Conditions (heat, light, electricity, catalyst, temperature, pressure) go above or below the arrow.

key_terms.definition_md: An equation with correct formulae in which the atoms are not yet balanced.
The number written in front of a formula to balance an equation.
Total mass of the products equals the total mass of the reactants.
A substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up; written on the arrow.

sections.heading: 3. Combination and decomposition reactions
sections.body_md:
**Combination**: two or more reactants form a **single product**, $\ce{A + B -> AB}$.
- Quicklime and water (whitewash): $\ce{CaO(s) + H2O(l) -> Ca(OH)2(aq)}$ + heat. Over the next few days the slaked lime on the wall reacts with carbon dioxide in air to form a thin, shiny layer of calcium carbonate.
- Burning of coal and of hydrogen; ammonia + hydrogen chloride → white fumes of ammonium chloride.

**Decomposition**: a single reactant breaks into two or more simpler products, $\ce{AB -> A + B}$. It needs energy:
- **Thermal** (heat): limestone in a lime kiln; ferrous sulphate crystals (pale green → reddish-brown $\ce{Fe2O3}$, smell of burning sulphur); lead nitrate (brown fumes of nitrogen dioxide).
- **Electrolytic** (electricity): water with a few drops of dilute sulphuric acid → hydrogen at the cathode (−) and oxygen at the anode (+), **2 : 1 by volume**. Hydrogen burns with a pop; oxygen relights a glowing splinter.
- **Photolytic** (light): white silver chloride turns grey in sunlight; silver bromide behaves the same (black-and-white photography). Silver salts are stored in dark bottles.

key_terms.definition_md: Two or more reactants combine to form a single product.
A single reactant breaks down into two or more simpler products.
Decomposition brought about by heat.
Decomposition brought about by passing an electric current.
Decomposition brought about by light.

sections.heading: 4. Displacement, double displacement and precipitation
sections.body_md:
**Displacement**: a more reactive element replaces a less reactive one from its compound, $\ce{A + BC -> AC + B}$.

Reactivity series (most → least reactive): K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, Pb, [H], Cu, Hg, Ag, Au.
- Iron nail in copper sulphate: blue → pale green; reddish-brown copper coats the nail.
- Zinc in copper sulphate: blue → colourless; copper deposits.
- Copper in silver nitrate: solution turns blue; shiny silver deposits.
- Copper in iron sulphate: **no reaction** (copper is less reactive than iron).

**Double displacement**: two compounds exchange ions, $\ce{AB + CD -> AD + CB}$. If a product is insoluble it forms a **precipitate** (a **precipitation reaction**).
- Sodium sulphate + barium chloride → **white** barium sulphate.
- Lead nitrate + potassium iodide → **yellow** lead iodide.
- Silver nitrate + sodium chloride → **white, curdy** silver chloride.
- Copper sulphate + sodium hydroxide → **blue** copper hydroxide.
- Acid + base (neutralisation) is double displacement **without** a precipitate.

key_terms.definition_md: A more reactive element displaces a less reactive element from its compound.
A list of metals in decreasing order of reactivity.
Two compounds exchange their ions (partners) to form two new compounds.
A reaction that produces an insoluble solid (precipitate).

sections.heading: 5. Exothermic and endothermic reactions
sections.body_md:
**Exothermic** reactions give out heat (surroundings warm up): burning of fuels (LPG, coal), respiration, quicklime + water, decomposition of vegetable matter into compost, neutralisation.

**Endothermic** reactions take in heat (energy must be supplied, or the surroundings cool): thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate, photosynthesis, electrolysis of water. Most decomposition reactions are endothermic because energy is needed to break the reactant apart.

**Respiration** is exothermic: glucose from digested food is oxidised in cells, releasing the energy that keeps us warm and active. **Photosynthesis** is endothermic: plants absorb light energy and store it in glucose.

key_terms.definition_md: A reaction in which heat is released to the surroundings.
A reaction in which heat (or other energy) is absorbed from the surroundings.

sections.heading: 6. Oxidation and reduction (redox)
sections.body_md:
- **Oxidation**: gain of oxygen **or** loss of hydrogen.
- **Reduction**: loss of oxygen **or** gain of hydrogen.
- They always occur together: a **redox** reaction.
- **Oxidising agent**: gives oxygen or removes hydrogen; it is itself **reduced**.
- **Reducing agent**: removes oxygen or gives hydrogen; it is itself **oxidised**.

Heating brown copper in air gives black copper oxide (copper oxidised). Passing hydrogen over hot copper oxide turns it brown again (copper oxide reduced, hydrogen oxidised).

**Method for any redox question**: (1) find the substance that loses oxygen/gains hydrogen → reduced, and it is the oxidising agent; (2) find the substance that gains oxygen/loses hydrogen → oxidised, and it is the reducing agent.

key_terms.definition_md: Gain of oxygen or loss of hydrogen by a substance.
Loss of oxygen or gain of hydrogen by a substance.
The substance that supplies oxygen or removes hydrogen; it is reduced.
The substance that removes oxygen or supplies hydrogen; it is oxidised.

sections.heading: 7. Corrosion and rancidity
sections.body_md:
**Corrosion**: a metal is slowly attacked by substances around it such as air, moisture and acids.
- Iron → reddish-brown **rust** (hydrated iron(III) oxide, $\ce{Fe2O3.xH2O}$). Rusting needs **both oxygen and water**; salt water speeds it up.
- Copper → green coating (basic copper carbonate); silver → black coating (silver sulphide).
- Prevention: painting, oiling/greasing, **galvanising** (zinc coating), chrome plating, alloying (stainless steel).

**Rancidity**: oxidation of fats and oils in food, giving a bad smell and taste.
- Prevention: airtight containers, **flushing packets with nitrogen**, adding antioxidants, refrigeration, keeping food away from light.

key_terms.definition_md: The slow damage of a metal by air, moisture or chemicals around it.
Reddish-brown hydrated iron(III) oxide formed when iron corrodes.
Coating iron or steel with a thin layer of zinc to prevent rusting.
Oxidation of fats and oils in food, causing a change in smell and taste.
A substance added to food to slow down oxidation of fats and oils.
